overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 6
overview.pill: Calculating and Interpreting Measures of Center and Variability
overview.text: Students use a calculator to compute the mean and the standard deviation of a data set and compare the variability of data sets where the differences in variability are less obvious than in previous lessons. Additionally, students continue to refine their knowledge of standard deviation and how it measures a typical deviation from the mean.
outcomes: Students calculate the standard deviation of a sample with the aid of a calculator.
Students compare the relative variability of distributions using standard deviations.
overview.teacherInsight: Emphasize precise mathematical definitions and multiple problem-solving representations. Encourage students to check the reasonableness of their numerical solutions.

exitTicket.title: Lesson 6 Exit Ticket: Interpreting the Standard Deviation
exitTicket.prompt:
Exit Ticket

Use the statistical features of your calculator to find the mean and the standard deviation to the nearest tenth of a data set of the miles per gallon from a sample of five cars.

24.9 24.7 24.7 23.4 27.9

Suppose that a teacher plans to give four students a quiz. The minimum possible score on the quiz is 0, and the maximum possible score is 10.

What is the smallest possible standard deviation of the students' scores? Give an example of a possible set of four student scores that would have this standard deviation.

What is the set of four student scores that would make the standard deviation as large as it could possibly be? Use your calculator to find this largest possible standard deviation.
exitTicket.solution:
Use the statistical features of your calculator to find the mean and the standard deviation to the nearest tenth of a data set of the miles per gallon from a sample of five cars.

24.9 24.7 24.7 23.4 27.9

Mean: 25.1 miles per gallon, to the nearest tenth

Standard Deviation: 1.7 miles per gallon, to the nearest tenth

Suppose that a teacher plans to give four students a quiz. The minimum possible score on the quiz is 0, and the maximum possible score is 10.

What is the smallest possible standard deviation of the students' scores? Give an example of a possible set of four student scores that would have this standard deviation.

The minimum possible standard deviation is 0. This will come about if all the students receive the same score (e.g., if every student scores an 8 on the quiz).

What is the set of four student scores that would make the standard deviation as large as it could possibly be? Use your calculator to find this largest possible standard deviation.

0, 0, 10, 10

Standard Deviation: 5.77, to the nearest hundredth

problemSet.title: Official Worksheet: Problem Set & Practice
problemSet.description: Master Interpreting the Standard Deviation through authentic curriculum practice problems. Check your work using the expandable teacher solution key below.

problems.prompt:
At a track meet, there are three men's 100 m races. The times for eight of the sprinters are recorded to the nearest \frac{1}{10} of a second. The results of the three races for these eight sprinters are shown in the dot plots below.

Race 1

Race 2

Race 3

Remember that the size of the standard deviation is related to the sizes of the deviations from the mean. Without doing any calculations, indicate which of the three races has the smallest standard deviation of times. Justify your answer.
problems.solution: Race 3 has the smallest standard deviation because several race times are clustered around the mean.

problems.prompt: Which race had the largest standard deviation of times? (Again, don't do any calculations!) Justify your answer.
problems.solution: Race 2 has the largest standard deviation because the race times are spread out from the mean.

problems.prompt: Roughly what would be the standard deviation in Race 1? (Remember that the standard deviation is a typical deviation from the mean. So, here you are looking for a typical deviation from the mean, in seconds, for Race 1.)
problems.solution: Around 0.5—1.0 second would be a sensible answer.

problems.prompt:
Use your calculator to find the mean and the standard deviation for each of the three races. Write your answers in the table below to the nearest thousandth.

How close were your answers for parts (a)—(c) to the actual values?
problems.solution: Answers will vary based on students' responses.

problems.prompt:
A large city, which we will call City A, holds a marathon. Suppose that the ages of the participants in the marathon that took place in City A were summarized in the histogram below.

Make an estimate of the mean age of the participants in the City A marathon.
problems.solution: Around 40 years would be a sensible estimate.

problems.prompt: Make an estimate of the standard deviation of the ages of the participants in the City A marathon.
problems.solution: Between 8 and 15 years would be a sensible estimate.

problems.prompt:
A smaller city, City B, also held a marathon. However, City B restricts the number of people of each age category who can take part to 100. The ages of the participants are summarized in the histogram below.

Approximately what was the mean age of the participants in the City B marathon? Approximately what was the standard deviation of the ages?
problems.solution: Mean is around 53 years; standard deviation is between 15 and 25 years.

problems.prompt: Explain why the standard deviation of the ages in the City B marathon is greater than the standard deviation of the ages for the City A marathon.
problems.solution: In City A, there is greater clustering around the mean age than in City B. In City B, the deviations from the mean are generally greater than in City A, so the standard deviation for City B is greater than the standard deviation for City A.
